assumedContext: SpaceX was private until 12 June 2026. It is now public, so this dossier is a public-equity analysis — but with only two quarters of reported results, the evidence base is far thinner than for an established listed company.

Sector recorded as infrastructure. The company genuinely spans three: launch (industrials), Starlink (consumer/enterprise subscription infrastructure) and xAI (software). All three profiles are applied.

No primary filing could be retrieved: every external domain is blocked by this environment egress proxy, including sec.gov. Findings rest on search-result summaries of the S-1, the Q2 2026 release and reputable press.

findings.claim: SpaceX listed on Nasdaq under SPCX on 12 June 2026 at a subscription price of USD 135, closing the first day at USD 161, up 19%. It trades at USD 147.95 as of 5 September 2026.
findings.label: FACT
findings.source: Wikipedia IPO page; CNBC 2026-08-10; TradingView/Investing.com quotes

findings.claim: In February 2026 SpaceX acquired xAI in an all-stock exchange, creating a combined entity valued at approximately USD 1.25 trillion — SpaceX at roughly USD 1tn and xAI at roughly USD 250bn. xAI holders received 0.1433 SpaceX shares per xAI share, with a cash alternative at USD 75.46.
findings.label: FACT

findings.claim: Pricing power in Starlink is a subscription list price set by SpaceX, and the evidence supports it: subscribers reached 12 million by mid-2026, roughly double a year earlier, with 1.7 million net additions in Q2 2026 alone.
findings.label: FACT

findings.claim: Approximately 85% of Starlink revenue is recurring, and the segment carries an estimated 63% EBITDA margin for 2026 — the economics of a subscription infrastructure business rather than a hardware vendor.
findings.label: CONSENSUS

findings.claim: In launch, pricing power derives from a near-monopoly on reusable capacity. SpaceX targeted 150+ Falcon 9 launches in 2026 and reached its 50th by 26 April, with booster reuse routinely exceeding 20 flights per vehicle.
findings.label: FACT

findings.claim: The principal competitor in connectivity, Amazon Kuiper, must launch on rivals' rockets including SpaceX's own Falcon 9 — effectively funding its competitor — and its FCC mandate to deploy 50% of a 3,236-satellite constellation by July 2026 was expected to be missed, creating regulatory risk for the challenger rather than the incumbent.
findings.label: FACT
findings.source: IBTimes competitor analysis; Bloomberg; FCC licence terms via press

findings.claim: Starlink operates a working constellation of approximately 10,280 satellites, a density no competitor is close to matching.
findings.label: FACT

findings.claim: Governance is the weakest element of the case. Control is concentrated with Elon Musk across an entity that acquired another Musk-controlled company in an all-stock deal it valued itself, three months before listing. The transaction was between related parties on both sides.
findings.label: ANALYST ESTIMATE
findings.source: Derived from the merger structure; D&O Diary commentary on the related-party character

findings.claim: Key-man exposure is unusually concentrated: the chief executive sets the technical roadmap, the capital allocation and the public narrative for launch, connectivity and AI simultaneously.
findings.label: ANALYST ESTIMATE

findings.claim: Regulatory dependence runs both ways and is material: spectrum and constellation licensing sit with the FCC and the ITU, launch licensing with the FAA, and a substantial share of launch revenue comes from NASA and defence customers.
findings.label: ANALYST ESTIMATE
findings.source: Derived from the regulatory structure of the industry

gaps.item: The S-1 and the first 10-Q, read in full
gaps.whyItMatters: Everything in this dossier rests on secondary summaries of a company with two quarters of public disclosure. For a mature company that is a weakness; for a three-month-old listing it is close to disqualifying for a committee decision.
gaps.resolvedBy: SEC EDGAR — currently blocked by this environment

gaps.item: The independent fairness process behind the xAI valuation
gaps.whyItMatters: USD 250bn of the combined entity's value was ascribed in a related-party all-stock deal. Whether an independent committee and a fairness opinion supported it determines how much of that USD 250bn a public investor should credit.

gaps.item: Segment-level pricing and churn for Starlink
gaps.whyItMatters: Subscriber growth is disclosed; ARPU trajectory and churn are not. A doubling of subscribers at falling ARPU is a materially different business from one at flat ARPU.

risks.text: Control is concentrated in one individual who set both sides of a USD 250bn related-party transaction three months before the listing.
The company has two quarters of public reporting, so there is no track record of guidance versus delivery against which to test an extremely aggressive revenue target.
Spectrum, constellation and launch licensing are all discretionary government permissions, and a substantial share of launch revenue is government-sourced.

catalysts.text: Q3 2026 results — the second public report, and the first test of the revenue trajectory
Full lockup expiry — the remaining share base becomes tradable

conclusions: The franchise is real and the pricing power is demonstrable in all three segments: Starlink doubled subscribers to 12 million with ~85% recurring revenue, launch runs a near-monopoly on reusable capacity at 150+ flights a year, and the AI segment grew 247%.
The competitive moat in connectivity is wide and getting wider. Kuiper must buy launches from SpaceX to compete with SpaceX, and was expected to miss its FCC deployment deadline.

The weakness is not competitive, it is governance. A related-party all-stock merger ascribed USD 250bn to xAI on both sides of a transaction controlled by the same person, three months before the listing.

This is a three-month-old public company with two quarters of reported results. Every normal public-market check on an aggressive valuation — track record, guidance history, analyst scrutiny over cycles — is weaker here than for any other company examined under this protocol.
Roughly 13 billion shares exist against 639 million floated at IPO, with the lockup fully expiring on 8 December 2026.
thesisImpact: Phase 1 establishes that the business quality question is largely settled in the company's favour and the governance question is not. That inverts the usual shape of this protocol: the risk here is not that the franchise fails, but that a genuinely exceptional franchise has been priced by a market with unusually little information and unusually weak checks.
